item.text: {"text":"[MQSA-TED (WSDM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01056) is a close fit: combines short/long attention queries with distillation of global item-transition patterns into embeddings. Its analysis finds transition counts useful when repeated transitions exist, but weak under sparsity—supporting a hybrid with SASRec rather than transition-only scoring. [Allegro’s two-tower system (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.03702v1) distinguishes substitute retrieval from complementary recommendations by modifying the query tower while retaining the target encoder. Lightweight content embeddings and sampled-softmax training are relevant; its complementary-category mappings, external annotations, prices and seller features exceed this task’s available inputs. [KGSCL (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107191) uses explicit Amazon substitution/complementarity edges for augmentation, so its relationship supervision is also unavailable here.\n\nA feasible adaptation, inferred from these approaches: retain SASRec and add an asymmetric transition score q(i)ᵀk(j), with separate source/target projections over item IDs plus pooled title/description token embeddings initialized randomly. Train on ordered training-history pairs with sampled negatives; share token parameters across items to support sparse products, and tune the transition contribution using macro validation HR@10. Compare against symmetric text similarity and an ID-only transition branch to establish whether direction and text add value. This is a proposed experiment, not a published benchmark result. Ordered interactions provide next-item supervision but do not establish complementarity, substitution, compatibility or ownership needs; describe learned relations as directional transitions unless independent labels exist."}
